content: 1. Individuals can generally be considered immune to measles unless specific epidemiological data suggests otherwise. 2. Administrative coverage estimates are derived from annual reports on routine vaccination coverage, including the first and second doses of measles-containing vaccines (MCV1 and MCV2) and supplementary immunization activity (SIA) coverage. These reports are submitted through the WHO/UNICEF Joint Reporting Form (JRF) on Immunization. Additionally, WHO/UNICEF national coverage estimates, which may differ from administrative reports, are also utilized. 3. Analysis of vaccination coverage should be available down to the third administrative level to ensure detailed assessment. 4. Population-based surveys, such as WHO 30-cluster surveys, Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), and UNICEF-sponsored Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), are valuable tools for assessing routine immunization and SIA coverage. 5. Rapid coverage assessments (RCAs), often conducted after mass vaccination campaigns, can provide additional data to evaluate local-level vaccination coverage. 6. Serological surveys, when appropriately designed and implemented, can offer detailed insights into immunity levels by birth cohort. However, limitations may arise from the sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value of laboratory tests used to detect measles immunoglobulin G (IgG). 7. The measles strategic planning tool can be employed to estimate immunity by birth cohort. 8. Additional data, such as outbreak duration, the number of transmission generations, the proportion of imported and import-related cases, and sero-epidemiological survey data, can inform models estimating effective reproduction numbers (R). 9. It is crucial to provide all evidence supporting population immunity levels, as all current estimation methods have inherent limitations. 10. Sustainability of national immunization programs, including resources for mass campaigns, is essential to maintain measles elimination. Verification of measles elimination should include an assessment of whether elimination can be sustained. 11. Evidence should highlight the strengths and weaknesses of national immunization programs in maintaining high and homogeneous vaccination coverage (≥95%) and high-quality surveillance. 12. Countries should prepare costed outbreak preparedness plans with appropriate budgets to respond to outbreaks caused by measles virus importations. 13. Measles elimination efforts should strengthen national immunization programs and surveillance systems while ensuring equitable immunization service delivery. 14. Sustainability assessments should translate into national action plans addressing identified programmatic gaps. 15. These assessments may be integrated into broader program reviews and feasibility assessments for new immunization initiatives, contributing to overall health system strengthening. 16. Genotyping evidence is critical to verify the interruption of measles virus transmission. The absence of previously endemic measles virus strains for over 12 months aligns with elimination. 17. Genotypes endemic to the Western Pacific Region in 2012 included D9 (Philippines, Malaysia) and H1 (China). Other genotypes, such as D4 and D8, are frequently imported from Europe and South-East Asia. 18. Virological surveillance and genetic sequencing, combined with robust epidemiological investigations, are essential to differentiate endemic from imported and import-related cases and to determine if endemic transmission has been re-established. 19. A wide range of virological analyses over multiple years, with an emphasis on the most recent five years, supports the achievement of measles elimination. 20. The Regional Verification Commission (RVC) is the sole body authorized to verify measles elimination in countries, areas, and the region as a whole. 21. Subregional Verification Committees (SRVCs) and National Verification Committees (NVCs) assess measles elimination status within their borders, determine readiness for verification, and assist ministries of health in preparing necessary documentation for submission to the RVC. 22. The RVC, SRVCs, and NVCs provide guidance to national immunization programs and vaccine-preventable disease surveillance units regarding verification requirements. 23. The RVC contributes its evolving knowledge to global measles eradication efforts and evaluates updates recommended by the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on Immunization. 24. RVC members are appointed by the WHO Regional Director for the Western Pacific and serve two-year terms, with the possibility of renewal. They must complete and sign a declaration of interest form before each meeting to avoid conflicts of interest. 25. NVC members are appointed by their respective ministries of health and report to the RVC. They should ideally represent diverse areas of expertise, including epidemiology, pediatrics, public health, virology, and molecular biology. 26. The WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific serves as the secretariat for the RVC. SRVCs and NVCs may establish their own secretariats to provide evidence of measles elimination. 27. The RVC, SRVCs, and NVCs serve as advisory bodies on verification criteria and lines of evidence, while also advocating for measles elimination activities. 28. The RVC Chair leads the commission, presides over meetings, defines internal procedures, supervises documentation, and submits annual reports to the Regional Director. 29. SRVCs and NVCs advise ministries of health on verification requirements, compile and analyze relevant data, conduct field visits, and ensure the development of annual progress reports for submission to the RVC. 30. These committees also monitor progress toward rubella control and elimination, provide programmatic guidance, and advocate for measles elimination.
